newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia fixed-interest bond aimed at foreigners.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia fixed-interest bond aimed at foreigners.

text.p: Russia launched trading of three-year fixed-interest government bonds on Monday as the City of Moscow won high ratings for its planned Eurobond next month and several major Russian banks were upgraded.
The new bonds and the ratings news were further signs that Russia's fixed-income markets are developing and will make them more attractive to foreign investors, bond analysts said.

Foreign investors have already poured billions of dollars in to Russian Treasury bills in recent months, driving yields below 30 percent from 200 percent early last year, while Russia's own $1 billion Eurobond, the biggest ever debut sovereign issue, was heavily oversubscribed last November.
Bond dealers said the new fixed-interest securities would mainly attract interest from foreigners, as local banks are still too small to invest in three-year paper.
The Finance Ministry has so far issued discount GKO Treasury bills and longer-term floating rate OFZ bonds, with maturities of up to two years, whose coupons are tied to T-bill yields.

The Central Bank offered a first 500 billion rouble ($88 million) tranche of 20 percent fixed-rate OFZ bonds on Monday, selling about 4.26 billion roubles of paper at 92.20 to yield 24.55 percent annual, Deputy Central Bank Chairman Andrei Kozlov told Reuters.
He said the paper was aimed mainly at foreign investors.
"We expect foreign investors to pay more attention to OFZ fixed interest bonds," he said.
"When the coupon does not change for several years, it is easy to plan and forecast profit and income. One can invest in the paper and hold it long enough without risk."

The Finance Ministry issued the bonds in June with a volume of 3.8 trillion roubles, sold it to the state-owned savings bank Sberbank, which later sold it to the Central Bank. The bonds were not sold on the open market because of the volatile trading conditions around last summer's presidential election.
"Russian participants' interest will be weak," Natsionalny Rezervny Bank dealer Stanislav Litvinov said. "All the paper is in one set of hands and the discount will not be very big."
"The Central Bank has no need to sell the paper, it wants to set up a market for non-residents."
But Sergei Ivanov, fixed-income trader at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow, said the market would not attract much attention from non-residents due to its low liquidity.
"Foreigners are mainly interested in paper which can be sold quickly," he said.
Kozlov said the market would become more liquid.

"Every day the Central Bank will quote the issue until we have placed 100-200 billion roubles so that the market can live on its own," he said. "After that we will maybe try to place the rest at auctions to raise liquidity. When the market is satiated the Finance Ministry will come and start issuing new issues."
Litvinov said Russian banks' funds were too limited and expensive to invest in long-term Russian paper.
Bank rating agency Thomson BankWatch said it had upgraded the long-term senior debt of four Russian banks -- Menatep, Vozrozhdeniye, Far Eastern and Rossiisky Kredit -- to B+ from B.
Ivanov said the rating improved Russia's banks' chances to raise funds by issuing promissory notes.
Thomson it was upgrading the banks in line with an improved sovereign rating for Russia of B+ instead of B.

At the same time the two big international rating agencies, Standard & Poor's and Moody's, assigned the City of Moscow's forthcoming Eurobond BB- and Ba2 respectively, the same as they allocated to Russia for its debut sovereign Eurobond last year.
Moscow officials say the capital's first Eurobond, to be lead-managed by CS First Boston and Nomura International, will be launched on March 15 to raise $400 million.

The ratings will also allow Moscow, which launched its municipal bond programme last week with a heavily oversubscribed offer of 10 billion roubles of six-month paper, to issue longer-dated domestic debt, George Nianias, an adviser to the city's debt programme, said. Russian Roubles)
